explanations.explanation: This neuron is simply picking out the dash/hyphen‐style punctuation token (the “–” or “-” connector) used in date ranges, compound words, title separators, etc.

This neuron is simply firing on particular character-sequence “subword” chunks (BPE/morpheme-like n-grams) wherever they appear—e.g. leg in Elegance, read in Dreadlocks, usp in suspension, itable in editable, etc. It’s an orthographic detector of these recurring subword fragments, not a higher-level semantic concept.
This neuron lights up on hedging/approximation constructions that use “or” to qualify degree (e.g. “more or less,” “little or no”), marking a vague or approximate quantity rather than a precise one.

This neuron fires on sentence-level discourse adverbs or connectors that signal an additive or contrastive continuation—especially things like “as well,” “too,” “altogether,” or “however” when used to wrap up or append to the preceding clause.

This neuron flags the little “linking” words that set up paired or ranged items—i.e. conjunctions/prepositions like “to,” “and,” or “or” when they connect two similar entities (e.g. “year to year,” “front and rear,” “S1 or S2,” “day to day,” etc.).
This feature fires sharply at sentence‐ or segment‐boundaries—e.g. the period (or newline/bullet) ending one item and the very first word of the next.

This feature acts as a “foreign‐script detector,” firing on contiguous spans of non-Latin text (names, dates, bibliographic entries, etc.) in languages like Russian (Cyrillic), Chinese, Korean (Hangul), Arabic, Devanagari, Bengali, Tamil, and so on.

This neuron lights up on the standard “scaffolding” or boilerplate wrappers around user‐generated content—things like “This entry was posted on…,” “Last edited by… at…,” “Published/Updated:…,” “Shop our wide selection…,” “Authors:…,” “Cite:…,” “Please note:…,” FAQ intros, affiliate disclaimers, phone numbers, part codes, etc. In short, it flags the meta‐data headers, footers and call-to-action templates that surround the main text rather than the substantive prose itself.

This feature fires on the “slash” as a delimiter—i.e. it marks tokens immediately following “/” (whether “or” in “and/or,” date components in “MM/DD/YY,” part-of-abbrev’s like “Bail/Anticipatory,” URL paths, etc.), signaling a slash‐separated alternative or structured sequence.

This neuron flags “header-style” tokens—i.e. words or abbreviations that carry title- or metadata-type capitalization (proper names, acronyms, dates/months, section headings, company tags, etc.). It lights up whenever the model sees a token that looks like the start of a named entity, acronym, or formatted header.

This feature fires at paragraph‐ or section‐level boundaries—peaking on the very first and last tokens of a block (titles, salutations, headings or closing periods) to mark where one paragraph ends and the next begins.

This neuron fires on functional‐relation words that introduce causality or capability in a sentence—e.g. “due to,” “able to,” “keeps…” or negation like “not support”—marking clauses that express cause, effect, or an entity’s ability.

This neuron is essentially a “boundary‐punctuation” detector—it fires on the final period or question‐mark that closes off a sentence, title, date, honorific or abbreviation (e.g. Gov. , Sen. , U.S. , end-of-sentence periods/question marks).

This feature fires on sentence-initial proper-noun tokens—especially first names or other named-entity headings—marking the introduction of a person (or other entity) at the start of a biographical or news‐style entry.
This neuron flags out‐of‐vocabulary or foreign‐script characters (in practice the “�” replacement symbol and other non-Latin/ASCII tokens).
This neuron is essentially a detector for the English negative-auxiliary contraction “doesn’t” (the “doesn’t/doesn’t” form of negation on third-person singular verbs).

This neuron lights up on formal, bureaucratic register—specifically on common written discourse connectors (“as well as,” “as soon as,” etc.) and on the subword suffixes that form abstract nouns (-ance/-ence/-ency, ‑ment, ‑ness, etc.).

The feature fires on the very first token of a bold-emphasized heading or section title (e.g. the word immediately following “**” at the start of a line), i.e. it marks the opening word of markdown-style headings and other structurally emphasized document titles.
This feature detects the middle two-digit number in parenthesized date/time strings (e.g. the day-of-month in “(July 22, 2016)” or the minute in “at 12:16 pm”).
The feature is a “named‐entity subword” detector: it fires on the distinctive core pieces of people’s and place names, brand/product titles, classification labels and other domain-specific keywords.
